title: A spacetime magnifying glass
caption: The galaxy cluster Abell S1077, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Abell S1077 · constellation Piscis Austrinus · about z=0.312 (redshift) away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Stretched stripes resembling scratches on a lens run through this picture of the galaxy cluster Abell S1077. They are really galaxies behind the cluster, whose light has been heavily distorted by its gravity.

Galaxy clusters are large groups of galaxies, each containing millions of stars, and they are the largest structures in the Universe held together by gravity. So much matter is packed into them that they warp spacetime and bend the path of light passing through. Sometimes this works like a magnifying lens, revealing objects behind the cluster that would otherwise be too faint to detect from Earth.

Astronomers combine Hubble with gravitational lensing to look far back in time to the early Universe. One record holder, the galaxy MACS0647-JD, was seen by Hubble and the Spitzer Space Telescope through a similar lens in the cluster MACS J0647.7+7015. Its light took 13.3 billion years to reach us.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3 observed the cluster in near-infrared light, from 814 nm to 1.6 μm. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the lensed background galaxies are far too faint to see without Hubble.
